description: Hi I am an M.Tech AI and B.Tech CSE student working on the "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots" challenge. My goal is to build a smart AI-driven geospatial dashboard that merges NASA's MODIS and VIIRS thermal datasets, removes duplicate detections, and predicts wildfire spread patterns. I specialize in Python, Machine Learning, and data visualization. Looking for passionate teammates (or working solo) skilled in frontend/UI, data analysis, or storytelling to build an impactful prototype
summary: FireHarmonize combines NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from two different sensor families, MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21), into one comparable burning-activity picture of India and its surroundings from January 2012 to November 2026. Because the sensors differ in pixel size, overpass time and confidence scales, we never simply concatenate them: records are cleaned, placed on a common 0.25° grid and daily time step, and each satellite is normalised by its own typical activity. The result is our Harmonized Fire Activity Index (HFAI), a derived metric, not an official NASA product. The web app shows an interactive map, a burning calendar, historical and seasonal trends, anomaly detection against each month's historical median, a MODIS vs VIIRS comparison, and CSV download, helping researchers, land managers and responders see when and where burning is unusual.
details:
What it does: FireHarmonize turns 12.6 million valid hotspots (nominal + high confidence) from NASA FIRMS into a single, comparable burning-activity record.

How it works: (1) Cleaning: invalid coordinates, duplicates and non-vegetation-fire rows are removed. (2) Harmonization: hotspots are grouped on a common 0.25° grid and daily intervals, sensor source is preserved, and each satellite's activity is scaled by its own 95th-percentile daily value so MODIS and VIIRS curves are comparable. (3) HFAI is computed daily and monthly for nine regions of India. (4) Anomaly detection compares current activity with the median of the same period in other years using a robust z-score based on Median Absolute Deviation; days above a threshold (robust z >= 3.5) are flagged.

Web app: Dashboard, interactive Leaflet map (fire-active days per cell, or difference from the average of other years), burning calendar, historical/seasonal analysis, anomaly detection, sensor comparison (monthly MODIS vs VIIRS Pearson r = 0.98), and CSV download for any region and date range.

Benefits and impact: Gives researchers, land managers and emergency responders one consistent view of historical fire patterns and where current burning departs from normal.

Tools: Python (Pandas, NumPy) for processing; Plotly.js and Leaflet for visualisation; static HTML/CSS/JavaScript site hosted on GitHub Pages.

Limitations: HFAI is our own derived index and is not an official NASA product. Hotspot counts represent satellite detections, not burned area. Data runs through 2 November 2026.
